asDecan.p: Each sign is cut into three ten-degree decans, each with its own planet. Your Sun sits in the middle one of Pisces, ten to nineteen degrees, and the Golden Dawn gives it to Jupiter. It's a neat fit, because Jupiter is also the traditional ruler of Pisces (modern astrology gives it Neptune). So in your ten degrees Jupiter runs both the sign and the slice, at home and with nothing to prove, and the middle of a sign is where it's most settled anyway. Jupiter enlarges whatever it touches. Pisces is mutable water, the sign that takes on the mood of whoever's nearby, and with Jupiter in charge that mood is usually a good one, and it spreads. Behind you is Saturn's Eight of Cups, the figure heading off into the dark, and ahead is Mars and the Ten, where a bit more push comes in. The Moon is still your Sun card, as the Major for all of Pisces. The Nine is what your ten degrees do with it.

You're usually the most relaxed person in the room, and people pick up on it before they could say why. A friend leaves your text on read for two days and it doesn't occur to you that they're annoyed. You assume they're busy, and they usually were. In a meeting where a deadline's just been missed and everyone's gone tight around the mouth, you're the one who says it'll be alright, and people believe you. A wet Saturday with the plans cancelled doesn't bother you at all. You go to the market, buy too much bread, and call it a good day. I see this a lot with mid-Pisces Suns. People call it luck, and Jupiter's own Major is the Wheel of Fortune, so they're not far wrong. Some of it is just that you expect things to go well and act like it.

Someone offers to pay for dinner and you let them. Your manager says the report was excellent and you say thanks and mean it, where most people deflect, or start working out in their heads how to pay it back. That's rarer than it sounds, and it's the side of your generosity people don't tend to notice, because it looks like taking. At a birthday where the person being celebrated is squirming through the speeches, you're the one who makes it easy for them to sit there and be fussed over, mostly by showing them how. You have the second slice of cake and they relax a bit. It comes from Jupiter being at home in your sign. Jupiter assumes there's more where that came from, so accepting something doesn't feel like a debt to you, and you don't leave other people feeling they owe you either.

Being content can turn into not wanting to hear bad news, yours or anyone else's. A friendship has gone one-sided over the last year and you keep describing it as lovely, because the other option is a conversation, and conversations like that make you feel slightly ill. Have a look at the man on the card, arms folded in front of all those cups. He's pleased, and he's also a bit shut. You can be like that when things are going well, a little smug about it if you're honest, and the friend who's having a terrible year picks up on it and decides not to mention the terrible year. You find out months later, from someone else, and you're hurt they didn't tell you. Mostly they didn't want to spoil your good mood.

When something goes badly wrong, a redundancy, a death in the family, a partner packing a bag, your first reflex is faith. It'll work out, it happened for a reason, something better's coming, and you say it to everyone, including people who needed to hear that it was awful. For a few days you mostly believe it. About a week later the feeling leaks out sideways, through comfort. A bottle of wine most nights where there used to be a glass, takeaway four nights running, something expensive bought at one in the morning. Jupiter at home is generous with everything, the soothing included. The people close to you often don't realise anything's wrong, which costs them too, since they never get a turn looking after you. What helps is letting one person see it. Tell them it's bad, in those words, and let them bring the food for once.

Where it gets interesting is who you fall for. Jupiter is the planet of faith, and in your sign it believes in people, sometimes well before they've earned it. You meet someone a bit lost, the one at the party who's had a rough year, and you can see exactly who they'd be with some warmth and backing, so you supply it. For a while that's lovely for both of you. It gets tiring when you've become the main source of their good mood and you're still waiting for the person you saw in them to turn up. The ones that last for mid-Pisces people are usually with someone who was fairly happy before you arrived, with their own friends and their own Saturday plans. To be honest, that can feel a bit flat at first, because there's nothing to fix. Give it a few months before you decide.

You're good at work where the whole point is that people leave in a better mood than they arrived in. Running a guesthouse or a wine bar, fundraising for a charity, leading tours, the pastoral side of a school, a bookshop people visit partly to talk to you. Jupiter rules teaching as well, so you're often the one who gets a team to think the thing can actually be done, and when you ask for money for a cause, people tend to give it. Where you slip is detail. You'd sooner give the discount than chase the invoice, and you'll agree to an extra project because it sounds fun, then find it's due the same week as three others. A manager who handles the numbers, or a business partner who's properly fussy about them, frees you up. Let them have the spreadsheet, and read the summary they send you.

At twenty this slice often looks like being everyone's favourite person and never quite knowing where the week went. You say yes to every plan, lend what you haven't got, and the good feeling carries you through most of it. By the mid-thirties there's usually been one stretch where the comfort went too far, a debt, a relationship you stayed in because it was pleasant enough, a habit you didn't much like the look of. Most people with this decan sort it out without much drama, because feeling well matters to them and they notice quickly when they don't. The fifties are often good years here. The contentment has taken some knocks and it's sturdier for them, and it depends less on everything going your way. People are often surprised, round about then, by how many of the friends they were kind to at twenty-five are still around.

Once a month, pick an evening and put your bank balance and your calendar side by side, with a cup of tea and nothing else going on. Write down one thing you've been telling yourself is fine without checking. Just one. Then check it within the week, whether it's the credit card, the friend who's gone quiet, or the dentist appointment you keep moving. Most of the time it really is fine. Now and then it isn't, and then you've found it while it's still small.
